title: What are the JPA cascade types (PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, DETACH, REFRESH, ALL), what does each do, and how does cascade differ from orphan removal?
shortTitle: JPA cascade types — PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, DETACH, REFRESH, ALL

s1_definition.profdef: Cascade controls whether an EntityManager operation performed on a parent entity automatically PROPAGATES to its associated child entities. `CascadeType.PERSIST`: persisting the parent also persists new children. `CascadeType.MERGE`: merging the parent also merges children (copies detached state in). `CascadeType.REMOVE`: removing the parent also removes its children. `CascadeType.DETACH`: detaching the parent detaches children from the persistence context. `CascadeType.REFRESH`: refreshing the parent re-reads children from the database, discarding in-memory changes. `CascadeType.ALL` is shorthand for all of the above. You set cascade on the association, for example `@OneToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL)`. Orphan removal (`orphanRemoval = true`) is a RELATED but distinct feature: it deletes a child when it is REMOVED FROM THE PARENT'S COLLECTION, which `CascadeType.REMOVE` does not do (remove only cascades when the PARENT itself is deleted).
s1_definition.analogy: A customer (parent) at National Bank of India has orders (children). Cascade is the instruction "whatever I do to the customer, do the same to their orders." Save the customer and PERSIST cascades the new orders. Update a detached customer and MERGE cascades the updates. Close the customer account and REMOVE cascades to delete their orders. Orphan removal is a different, sharper rule: "if I tear one order slip out of the customer's folder, shred that one slip" — even though the customer still exists.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cascade propagates parent operations (PERSIST/MERGE/REMOVE/DETACH/REFRESH, or ALL) to children; orphanRemoval deletes a child when it leaves the parent's collection — REMOVE only fires when the whole parent is deleted.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cascade controls whether an EntityManager operation performed on a parent entity automatically PROPAGATES to its associated child entities. `CascadeType.PERSIST`: persisting the parent also persists new children. `CascadeType.MERGE`: merging the parent also merges children (copies detached state in). `CascadeType.REMOVE`: removing the parent also removes its children. `CascadeType.DETACH`: detaching the parent detaches children from the persistence context. `CascadeType.REFRESH`: refreshing the parent re-reads children from the database, discarding in-memory changes. `CascadeType.ALL` is shorthand for all of the above. You set cascade on the association, for example `@OneToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL)`. Orphan removal (`orphanRemoval = true`) is a RELATED but distinct feature: it deletes a child when it is REMOVED FROM THE PARENT'S COLLECTION, which `CascadeType.REMOVE` does not do (remove only cascades when the PARENT itself is deleted).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer (parent) at National Bank of India has orders (children). Cascade is the instruction "whatever I do to the customer, do the same to their orders." Save the customer and PERSIST cascades the new orders. Update a detached customer and MERGE cascades the updates. Close the customer account and REMOVE cascades to delete their orders. Orphan removal is a different, sharper rule: "if I tear one order slip out of the customer's folder, shred that one slip" — even though the customer still exists.

**One line to remember:** Cascade propagates parent operations (PERSIST/MERGE/REMOVE/DETACH/REFRESH, or ALL) to children; orphanRemoval deletes a child when it leaves the parent's collection — REMOVE only fires when the whole parent is deleted.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the lifecycle rules we needed for customers and their orders at National Bank of India.

Problem 1 — placing an order required persisting each child by hand. The first version persisted the customer and then persisted every order separately, which was verbose and easy to get wrong. This is exactly where `CascadeType.PERSIST` helps: persisting the customer cascades to its new orders in one call.

Problem 2 — reattaching an edited customer graph lost the order changes. An admin screen edited a customer and their orders as a detached graph (built from a request body), but merging the customer did not update the orders. This is exactly where `CascadeType.MERGE` helps: merging the customer copies the detached order changes into managed instances.

Problem 3 — closing an account left orphan orders. Deleting a customer did not delete their orders, leaving dangling rows. This is exactly where `CascadeType.REMOVE` helps: deleting the customer cascades the delete to their orders.

Problem 4 — cancelling a single order while keeping the customer did nothing. Removing an order from the collection did not delete it, because REMOVE only fires on parent deletion. This is exactly the REMOVE-versus-orphanRemoval distinction: `orphanRemoval = true` deletes a child the moment it leaves the collection, which is what cancellation needs.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `Customer` entity with `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)` so the full lifecycle is owned. There is an `Order` entity as the owning side. The `CustomerService`, annotated `@Transactional`, demonstrates four flows: creating a customer with orders (PERSIST cascade), merging a detached customer graph (MERGE cascade), cancelling one order (orphanRemoval), and closing the account (REMOVE cascade). Each flow logs which cascade fired. A test verifies the cascade annotations and that orphanRemoval and REMOVE are both configured, documenting their different triggers.

mvn clean package

# Run
java -jar target/customer-lifecycle-service-1.0.0.jar

# PERSIST cascade — create customer + orders in one save
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8369/api/v1/customers?customerId=CUST-AMIT&name=Amit%20Patel"
# SQL: INSERT customers(...) ; INSERT orders(...) ×2

# orphanRemoval — cancel ONE order, customer stays
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8369/api/v1/customers/CUST-RAJESH/orders/ORD-100
# SQL: DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id='ORD-100'

# REMOVE cascade — close account, delete customer + all orders
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8369/api/v1/customers/CUST-RAJESH
# SQL: DELETE FROM orders WHERE customer_id='CUST-RAJESH' ; DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id='CUST-RAJESH'

# Run tests
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input exercises all four lifecycle flows for customers and their orders.

Step 1 — PERSIST cascade. `createWithOrders("CUST-AMIT", "Amit Patel")` builds a new `Customer`, adds two orders through the sync helper, and calls `save` once. Because the association has `CascadeType.ALL` (which includes PERSIST), Hibernate inserts the customer and then both orders, setting `customer_id` on each. One save, three inserts.

Step 2 — MERGE cascade. An admin edits a customer and their orders as a detached graph and sends it back. `save` on an entity with an existing id performs a merge. Because `CascadeType.ALL` includes MERGE, Hibernate copies the detached order changes into managed instances and issues the corresponding updates. The whole graph reattaches in one call.

Step 3 — orphanRemoval. `cancelOrder("CUST-RAJESH", "ORD-100")` loads the customer with their orders, removes `ORD-100` from the collection via the helper, and saves. Because `orphanRemoval = true`, Hibernate sees the order left the owning collection and issues `DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 'ORD-100'`. The customer and their other orders remain. Note that `CascadeType.REMOVE` did NOT cause this — REMOVE only fires when the whole parent is deleted.

Step 4 — REMOVE cascade. `closeAccount("CUST-RAJESH")` loads the customer and calls `delete(customer)`. Because `CascadeType.ALL` includes REMOVE, Hibernate first deletes all the customer's orders, then deletes the customer. The cascade walks the object graph from parent to children.

Step 5 — the contrast is the key lesson. Removing a child from the collection (step 3) is governed by orphanRemoval; deleting the parent (step 4) is governed by REMOVE cascade. Both are needed for a complete aggregate lifecycle, and they fire on different triggers.

```
2026-10-24 00:54:40 INFO  CustomerService - [PERSIST cascade] saved CUST-AMIT and its new orders in one call
2026-10-24 00:54:40 FINE  CustomerService - INSERT customers ; INSERT orders ×2 (cascade PERSIST)
2026-10-24 00:54:40 INFO  CustomerService - [orphanRemoval] cancelled order ORD-100 — DELETEd, customer CUST-RAJESH remains
2026-10-24 00:54:40 INFO  CustomerService - [REMOVE cascade] closed CUST-RAJESH — deleted customer and all its orders
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ SIX CASCADE TYPES ═══

  PERSIST : em.persist(parent)  → INSERT parent, then INSERT new children
  MERGE   : em.merge(parent)    → UPDATE parent + copy detached children in
  REMOVE  : em.remove(parent)   → DELETE children, then DELETE parent
  DETACH  : em.detach(parent)   → detach parent + children (changes untracked)
  REFRESH : em.refresh(parent)  → re-read parent + children, discard in-memory edits
  ALL     : all five above

  ═══ CASCADE vs ORPHAN REMOVAL (different triggers!) ═══

  CascadeType.REMOVE:
    delete(customer)                 → DELETE all orders + customer
    (fires only when the PARENT is deleted)

  orphanRemoval = true:
    customer.getOrders().remove(order) → DELETE that one order
    (fires when a CHILD leaves the collection; customer STAYS)

  ═══ DANGER ZONES ═══
  cascade REMOVE/ALL on SHARED data → deleting one parent may delete data
                                       another parent still needs → DO NOT
  JPQL bulk DELETE                   → bypasses cascade entirely
  DB ON DELETE CASCADE               → separate mechanism from JPA cascade
```

  │  @OneToMany(cascade=ALL,        │◆──────▶│  @ManyToOne @JoinColumn        │
  │     orphanRemoval=true)         │        │  customer : Customer           │
  │  orders : List<Order>           │        └───────────────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Trigger Table ──
  create(customer)                    → PERSIST cascade  → INSERT orders
  save(detached customer graph)       → MERGE cascade    → UPDATE orders
  delete(customer)                    → REMOVE cascade   → DELETE orders + customer
  orders.remove(order)                → orphanRemoval    → DELETE that order

  ⚠ REMOVE ≠ orphanRemoval: REMOVE fires on parent delete; orphanRemoval on child-leaves-set.
  ⚠ Bulk JPQL DELETE bypasses cascade; ON DELETE CASCADE is a separate DB mechanism.
  Rule: cascade ALL + orphanRemoval for owned aggregates ONLY; never for shared data.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Cascade controls whether an operation on a parent entity automatically propagates to its associated children. PERSIST means saving the parent also inserts new children; MERGE means reattaching a detached parent also copies the children's detached state into managed instances; REMOVE means deleting the parent also deletes its children; DETACH means detaching the parent detaches the children so their changes stop being tracked; REFRESH means re-reading the parent also re-reads the children, discarding in-memory edits; and ALL is simply all five combined. I declare it on the association, for example OneToMany with cascade all, and I use ALL for a true aggregate where the children's whole lifecycle is owned by the parent.

The distinction interviewers probe is cascade REMOVE versus orphan removal, because they sound alike but fire on different triggers. Cascade REMOVE deletes the children only when I delete the parent itself. Orphan removal deletes a child the moment it is disassociated from the parent, that is, removed from the parent's collection, even while the parent continues to exist. In our customer and orders model at National Bank of India, creating a customer with orders uses the persist cascade, reattaching an edited customer graph uses the merge cascade, closing an account uses the remove cascade to delete the customer and all its orders, and cancelling a single order uses orphan removal so that one order is deleted while the customer stays. Both mechanisms together give the complete aggregate lifecycle.

The senior cautions I always give are that cascade follows the object graph, so applying REMOVE or ALL to a relationship pointing at shared reference data is dangerous because deleting one parent could delete data another parent still needs, so I cascade only to genuinely owned children. I also remember that cascade applies to EntityManager lifecycle operations and is completely bypassed by bulk JPQL delete statements, and that JPA cascade is a separate mechanism from a database-level on-delete-cascade foreign key, so I keep the two aligned to avoid confusion.
